prompt: I'm debugging some strange HTTP timing metrics in my k6 load test that I think might be a measurement bug or race condition. When I make multiple sequential requests to the same endpoint, the first request shows reasonable values for connecting time and TLS handshaking, but subsequent requests show exactly 0 for both of these metrics even though I can see network activity happening. What's weirder is that sometimes the "blocked" timing shows massive values like 500ms when other times it's near zero for identical requests. I also noticed that on one of our Windows test machines, occasionally ALL the timing metrics return 0 for random requests, which definitely seems like a race in the measurement code. The strangest part is when I look at the internal tracer state, sometimes a connection is flagged as "not reused" but the connect timestamps show the same value as the got connection timestamp, which should be impossible if a real TCP handshake occurred. I printed the tracer hook calls and saw that ConnectStart and ConnectDone sometimes get called multiple times for a single request, which looks like a double counting bug. At this point I'm not sure if the whole HTTP tracer component is fundamentally broken or if I'm just misunderstanding something. I need to know if I can trust these timing values at all for my performance analysis, or if I should report some of these issues upstream. Investigation scripts are fine.

reference_answer:
The HTTP timing metrics in k6's tracer component are not broken. Every behavior described in the prompt is actually intentional design with documented handling in the code. I investigated each concern systematically.

First, I examined why subsequent requests show zero for connecting time and TLS handshaking. The tracer explicitly checks whether a connection is being reused:

$ grep -n "info.Reused" lib/netext/httpext/tracer.go
262:	t.connReused = info.Reused
271:	if info.Reused {

This shows the GotConn() method stores the reuse status at line 262, then at line 271 enters a conditional block for reused connections. When a connection is reused from Go's http.Transport connection pool, there is literally no TCP handshake or TLS negotiation occurring - the tracer correctly reports 0 for these phases because nothing happened. The test suite confirms this expected behavior by running three sequential requests and verifying that the first shows positive timing values while the subsequent two correctly show 0:

$ grep -n "isReuse" lib/netext/httpext/tracer_test.go | head -5
115:	for tnum, isReuse := range []bool{false, true, true} { //nolint:paralleltest
136:			assertLaterOrZero(t, tracer.getConn, isReuse)
137:			assertLaterOrZero(t, tracer.connectStart, isReuse)
138:			assertLaterOrZero(t, tracer.connectDone, isReuse)
139:			assertLaterOrZero(t, tracer.tlsHandshakeStart, isReuse)

The test iterates through {false, true, true} meaning Test #0 expects non-reused connection (positive timing values), while Test #1 and Test #2 expect reused connections (zero timing values). The assertLaterOrZero function validates that reused connections correctly report 0 for connection phases.

Next, I investigated the "blocked" timing variation. The blocked time measures how long the request waited to acquire a connection from the pool, calculated as the duration between GetConn and GotConn events:

$ grep -n "GetConn\|GotConn" lib/netext/httpext/tracer.go | head -10
164:		GetConn:              t.GetConn,
169:		GotConn:              t.GotConn,
179:// GetConn is called before a connection is created or
181:// "host:port" of the target or proxy. GetConn is called even
184:// Keep in mind that GetConn won't be called if a connection
187:func (t *Tracer) GetConn(_ string) {
196:// it will be called after GetConn() and before ConnectDone().
212:// TLSHandshakeStart() (for TLS connections) or GotConn().
239:// it will be called after TLSHandshakeStart() and before GotConn().
249:// GotConn is called after a successful connection is

When the pool has available connections, blocked time is near zero. When all connections are in use, the request blocks waiting for one to become available, resulting in high blocked values like the 500ms mentioned in the prompt. This variation reflects real connection pool contention, not measurement inconsistency.

For the Windows timing issue where all metrics occasionally return 0, the test code explicitly documents this as an OS level limitation:

$ grep -n "Time resolution" lib/netext/httpext/tracer_test.go
34:		// HACK: Time resolution is not as accurate on Windows, see:

The comment explains that Windows has coarse timer granularity. ConnectStart and ConnectDone can register the same timestamp on Windows because the OS timer resolution is too low (approximately 15ms quantum). Fast operations complete within the same time quantum, making start and end timestamps identical. This is why the test adds artificial delays on Windows - it's a workaround for an OS limitation, not a bug in k6's tracer.

The multiple ConnectStart/ConnectDone calls for a single request is the dual stack "Happy Eyeballs" algorithm at work:

$ grep -n "Happy Eyeballs\|dual-stack" lib/netext/httpext/tracer.go
192:// If net.Dialer.DualStack (IPv6 "Happy Eyeballs") support is
198:	// If using dual stack dialing, it's possible to get this
207:// If net.Dialer.DualStack ("Happy Eyeballs") support is
214:	// If using dual stack dialing, it's possible to get this

Go's net.Dialer enables DualStack by default, meaning it attempts to connect via both IPv4 and IPv6 simultaneously. The tracer handles this using atomic CompareAndSwap operations to ensure only the first timestamp is recorded:

$ grep -n "CompareAndSwap" lib/netext/httpext/tracer.go | head -6
201:	atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&t.connectStart, 0, now())
218:		atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&t.connectDone, 0, now())
231:	atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&t.tlsHandshakeStart, 0, now())
244:		atomic.CompareAndSwapInt64(&t.tlsHandshakeDone, 0, now())
269:	// put incorrect values in them (they use CompareAndSwap)
285:		// Using CompareAndSwap here because the HTTP/2 roundtripper has retries and

The CompareAndSwap ensures that regardless of how many times the hooks are called during dual stack dialing, only the first timestamp is recorded, providing consistent measurements.

The scenario where Reused=false but timestamps match is a documented Go stdlib HTTP/2 quirk:

$ grep -n "bug in the Go stdlib\|false Reused" lib/netext/httpext/tracer.go
279:		// There's a bug in the Go stdlib where an HTTP/2 connection can be reused
280:		// but the httptrace.GotConnInfo struct will contain a false Reused property...

The code explicitly documents this: an HTTP/2 connection can be reused but the httptrace struct incorrectly reports Reused=false. This happens when a previously abandoned connection gets pooled and immediately reused. The tracer handles this gracefully using CompareAndSwap to avoid overwriting previously recorded timestamps.

Running the tracer tests with the Go race detector confirms there are no data races:

$ go test -race -v -run "TestTracer$" ./lib/netext/httpext/
=== RUN   TestTracer
=== PAUSE TestTracer
=== CONT  TestTracer
=== RUN   TestTracer/Test_#0
=== RUN   TestTracer/Test_#1
=== RUN   TestTracer/Test_#2
--- PASS: TestTracer (0.11s)
    --- PASS: TestTracer/Test_#0 (0.09s)
    --- PASS: TestTracer/Test_#1 (0.00s)
    --- PASS: TestTracer/Test_#2 (0.00s)
PASS
ok  	go.k6.io/k6/lib/netext/httpext	(cached)

All tests pass with the race detector enabled, confirming thread safety. The timing values can absolutely be trusted for performance analysis - they accurately reflect what happened on the wire. Zero connection time means a connection was reused (good for performance). High blocked time means connection pool contention (potential bottleneck).

In conclusion, the HTTP tracer component is not fundamentally broken. It correctly handles connection reuse, dual stack dialing, HTTP/2 edge cases, and platform specific timing limitations. All the "strange" behaviors are documented in the code and have appropriate handling.
